newsitem.title: UK: U.S. and European bonds go their separate ways.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and European bonds go their separate ways.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are set to fall further behind European bonds as evidence of U.S. economic strength continues to grow while the outlook for European economies remains stagnant, analysts said on Monday.

The spread between the yield on 10-year U.S. and German bonds was bloated by robust U.S. jobs data on Friday and analysts said the gap would stretch wider with the threat of tighter U.S. monetary policy.
"People are talking about the two geographical areas going in completely separate directions," said David Keeble, bond strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.

"In the U.S., we've got strong economic data coming out and people talking about rate hikes, whereas if you look over to France and Germany we've got very weak data, reversing some of the rate hike expectations," he said.
Latest British economic data were also relatively subdued, he added.

Analysts saw the chance for interest rate cuts this week in Italy, Spain and France, where some players were looking for the Bank of France to ease rates after its regular monetary policy meeting on Thursday.
"This week it is very likely we will get five basis points off the (French) intervention rate," said Sonia Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London.
In Germany too, strong unemployment figures last week underscored a bleak economic picture.
"A lot of people don't think Germany will cut rates again, but they certainly think that the bias, if anything, would be for lower interest rates," said Keeble.
Across the Atlantic, there is some talk of a rise in U.S. interest rates at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on February 4 and 5.
Gibbs said core Europe was unlikely to follow suit.

"In contrast to 1994 when the U.S. raised rates and Europe fell out of bed too, not only is the outlook for the U.S. more uncertain, but the outlook for Europe is completely different. There is no growth coming from anywhere," she said.
Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said recent U.S. data and price action in the Treasury market confirmed growth had not slowed as much as some had expected.
The data last week clearly showed that German and U.S. employment figures have diverged, he said, and this would soon be reflected in the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread.
"The risk for Treasuries is for them to go back to last year's lows," he said. "And in terms of the spread, we're looking for it to go out to 100 to 110 basis points on a one- to two-month view."
The 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread was at 87 basis points, or 0.87 percentage points, at the European mid-session.
Gibbs also said the spread differential had further to go.
"I wouldn't rule out as much as 90/95 basis points over the next few weeks and as much as 100 if we get some really very strong U.S. figures," she said.
U.S. December consumer prices, due on Tuesday, are forecast to be flat, but after Friday's employment data indicated an increase in wage pressures, there is a risk that CPI will come in higher.

Keeble said if the T-note/Bund spread got to 100 it would be time to buy Treasuries outright. He said European peripheral markets were looking extremely expensive against the U.S. which would ultimately have a supportive effect on the U.S. market.
In Europe, analysts predicted a period of fiscal consolidation which would tend to be positive for the bond market in terms of its overall impact on growth.
But further out, Nomura's Gibbs said U.S. bonds would strengthen as economic activity slowed later this year.
